unit.unitTitle: Media, Technology and Judging a Source
unit.unitOverview: Unit 9 taught you that the reporting verb carries the writer's judgement. This unit is about the layer above that: attribution that names nobody at all. Sources say, it is understood, critics argue — constructions that sound authoritative and can be entirely empty. It also covers the small words that pair and contrast, the markers that manage a conversation, and a method for judging whether a source is worth believing.
unit.learningPath:
Read and listen to the Lesson. There are four patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 1 is about what a sentence does not tell you.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is one story reported by two outlets.
Do the Practice. Practice 1 is the diagnostic — who is actually saying this?
Record yourself judging four sources.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.

visual.lectureScript:
In Unit 9 you learned that said, claimed and admitted carry the writer's opinion. This unit is about the layer above that, and it is the one that matters most for reading anything published.
First pattern: attribution that names nobody.
Sources say the decision has already been taken.
It is understood that two sites will close.
Critics argue that the policy has failed.
There are concerns about the timetable.
The move has been widely welcomed.
Every one of those sounds authoritative. Every one of them tells you nothing about who is speaking, and some of them may have nobody behind them at all.
So here is the test, and it works on anything you read. Ask: who exactly? And then: how many?
Sources say. Which sources? How many? Two people who work there and disagree with the decision is a source. So is the entire board. The phrase covers both.
Critics argue. Which critics? A named expert, or one person on the internet?
There are concerns. Whose concerns? Concerns is a noun with no owner — it is the abstract noun trick from Unit 8, applied to opinions.
Widely welcomed. Welcomed by whom? Widely is doing work that no evidence supports.
None of these constructions is dishonest in itself. Journalists genuinely need to protect sources, and it is standard practice for good reasons. What you need is not suspicion but the habit of noticing: this sentence has no person in it, and I cannot check it.
And there is a spectrum, which is worth learning.
Strongest: a named person with a named role, quoted directly. The regional manager, Dani Okonkwo, said…
Next: a named organisation. The company said…
Next: an unnamed but described source. A senior manager at the company said…
Next: an undescribed source. Sources say…
Weakest: no source at all. It is understood that…
Each step down removes something you could have checked. When a document uses the weakest form for its most important claim, that is worth noticing.
Second pattern: both, either and neither. Three small words for pairs, and they are easy to get almost right.
Both means the two together. Both sites are closing. Both of them agreed.
Either means one or the other. Either site could close. Either of them would do.
Neither means not one and not the other. Neither site is closing. Neither of them agreed.
The grammar points that catch people are these.
Both takes a plural verb. Both are closing.
Neither takes a singular verb in careful writing. Neither is closing. You will hear neither are constantly and it is not wrong in speech; in writing, singular is safer.
And the pairs: both … and, either … or, neither … nor. Both the cost and the timing. Either Tuesday or Thursday. Neither the cost nor the timing.
Neither takes nor, not or. That is the one to remember.
And there is a useful negative point. Neither already contains the negative, so you do not add another. Neither of them agreed, not neither of them didn't agree.
Third pattern: discourse markers. These are the small words that manage a conversation rather than adding information.
Actually. It corrects gently or introduces something mildly surprising. Actually, I think it was Thursday. It is one of the most useful words in spoken English and it does no work at all in a report.
In fact. It strengthens or corrects more firmly. In fact, the figures have doubled.
Mind you. It concedes something that partly undercuts what you just said. It is expensive. Mind you, it lasts twice as long.
To be fair. Similar, and slightly warmer. To be fair, they did apologise.
Anyway. It closes a digression or ends a topic.
The thing is. It introduces the real problem, and it usually signals that everything before it was preamble.
These are almost entirely spoken. Putting them in formal writing is a register error, and leaving them out of speech makes you sound like a document. That is the whole point of the group: they are how English speech signals what is happening in the conversation, and they carry no meaning you could paraphrase.
Fourth pattern: judging a source.
Four questions, and they take about thirty seconds.
Who is saying it? A named person, an organisation, or nobody. That is card 1.
How do they know? Were they there, did they see the document, or are they reporting what somebody else said? A source repeating another source is not a second source.
What would they gain? Everybody has an interest and having one does not make somebody wrong. But knowing what it is tells you which parts to check.
And: does anybody independent say the same? Two outlets both quoting the same press release are not two sources. Corroboration means an independent path to the same fact.
Those four questions are the whole method, and the fourth is the one people skip.
One last thing that is specific to how information reaches you now. What you see is selected — by an algorithm, by an editor, by whoever you follow. That selection is invisible and it is not neutral. So there is a fifth question worth asking occasionally: what would I not be seeing? It has no reliable answer, and asking it is still better than assuming the answer is nothing.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: Who Exactly, and How Many?
readings.passageScript:
Sources say the decision has already been taken.
It is understood that two sites will close.
Critics argue that the policy has failed.
There are concerns about the timetable.
The move has been widely welcomed.
Every one of those sounds authoritative and none of them tells you who is speaking. Some may have nobody behind them at all.
Two questions handle all of them. Who exactly? And how many?
Sources say. Which sources? Two colleagues who disagree with the decision would satisfy that phrase. So would the entire board. It covers both and distinguishes neither.
Critics argue. Which critics? A named specialist and one anonymous account are both critics.
There are concerns. Whose? Concerns is an abstract noun with no owner — the Unit 8 trick, applied to opinions instead of actions.
Widely welcomed. By whom, and how do you know it was wide?
None of this is dishonest in itself, and that matters. Journalists genuinely need to protect people who would lose their jobs for speaking, and unattributed sourcing exists for real reasons. What you need is not suspicion but a habit: noticing that this sentence contains no person and cannot be checked.
There is a spectrum, and it is worth learning as a ladder.
Strongest: a named person with a named role, quoted directly. The regional manager, Dani Okonkwo, said…
Then: a named organisation. The company said…
Then: an unnamed but described source. A senior manager at the company said…
Then: an undescribed source. Sources say…
Weakest: no source at all. It is understood that…
Every step down removes something you could have checked.
And here is the practical use of the ladder. Look at where a piece puts its most important claim. A report that names people for the uncontroversial facts and uses it is understood for the central allegation has told you something about how solid that allegation is.

readings.title: Repeating Is Not Corroborating
readings.passageScript:
Four questions judge a source, and they take about thirty seconds.
Who is saying it? A named person, a named organisation, or nobody. That is the ladder.
How do they know? Were they present, did they see the document, or are they passing on what somebody else said? This distinction is routinely lost. A person who heard about it is not a witness, and a report that says a source familiar with the matter is often describing exactly that.
What would they gain? Everybody has an interest, and having one does not make somebody wrong — that is worth stating plainly, because the opposite assumption is lazy. What an interest tells you is which parts of the account to check hardest: the parts that happen to favour the person giving it.
And the fourth, which almost everybody skips: does anybody independent say the same thing?
This is where the most common error in reading news lives.
Seeing a claim in four places feels like corroboration. Usually it is not. Four outlets carrying the same story within an hour of each other are, in most cases, four outlets carrying one press release, one briefing, or one agency wire. That is one source printed four times.
Corroboration means an independent path to the same fact. A second witness who was also there. A document that exists regardless of what anybody says. A second organisation that went and looked.
The test is practical: ask how each outlet would have found this out. If the answer is the same route in every case, you have one source.
There is a fifth question, and it is different in kind because it has no answer. What am I not seeing?
What reaches you has been selected — by an editor, by an algorithm, by the people you follow. That selection is invisible from inside it, and it is not neutral: it is optimised for something, usually attention.
You cannot solve this. But asking the question occasionally is better than assuming the answer is nothing, and one concrete thing does help: look at somebody else's feed sometime, and notice how little of it you have seen.

readings.setting: Two outlets reporting the same company statement on the same afternoon.
readings.passageScript:
REPORT ONE - Northfield Business Weekly

  MERIDIAN TO CLOSE TWO SITES

  Meridian Freight confirmed yesterday
  that it will close its Eastbourne and
  Millbrook depots in September, with the
  loss of 84 jobs.

  In a statement, the company said the
  closures followed \"a sustained fall in
  regional volumes\" and that affected
  staff would be offered redeployment
  \"where practicable\".

  Aisha Rahman, regional officer for the
  transport union, said the union had
  been given nine days' notice and would
  be seeking a full consultation period.

  Meridian's most recent published
  accounts show regional volumes down 11
  per cent over two years.

-----------------------------------------

  REPORT TWO - a news aggregator

  MERIDIAN AXES 84 JOBS IN SHOCK MOVE

  Sources say the decision to close two
  Meridian depots had already been taken
  months ago, despite the company's claim
  that it followed falling demand.

  It is understood that further closures
  may follow, and there are growing
  concerns among staff about the future
  of the remaining sites.

  Critics argue the company has
  prioritised shareholders over workers.
  The move has been widely condemned.

  Meridian did not respond to a request
  for comment.

grammar.sourceFile: Grade 7 Unit 8, Grade 7 Unit 9; Grade 8 Unit 8
grammar.title: Attribution that names nobody
grammar.explanation: Unit 9 covered the verbs that carry judgement. This is the layer above: constructions that sound authoritative and contain no person at all.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THE CONSTRUCTIONS
  Sources say...
  It is understood that...
  Critics argue that...
  There are concerns about...
  The move has been widely welcomed.
  A source close to the matter said...

TWO QUESTIONS HANDLE ALL OF THEM
  WHO exactly?   HOW MANY?

  \"Sources say\" is satisfied by two
  colleagues who disagree, and by the
  entire board. It distinguishes neither.

THE LADDER - strongest to weakest
  1 named person + role, quoted
  2 named organisation
  3 unnamed but DESCRIBED source
  4 undescribed source (\"sources say\")
  5 no source at all (\"it is understood\")

  each step down removes something you
  could have CHECKED.

THE PRACTICAL USE
  look at where the piece puts its MOST
  IMPORTANT claim on that ladder.

NOT DISHONEST IN ITSELF
  sources need protecting. The skill is
  NOTICING, not suspecting.
grammar.workedExample:
You read: sources say the decision had already been taken months ago.
1. Apply the first question. Who exactly? The sentence does not say, and it does not describe them either.
2. Apply the second. How many? Sources is plural, which could mean two. It could also mean two people who heard the same rumour.
3. Place it on the ladder. No name, no organisation, no description — that is level four.
4. Now the practical step. Is this the piece's central claim? Yes: it contradicts the company's stated reason. So the most contested claim in the report has the weakest attribution in it.
That is a finding, and it is not an accusation. The claim may be true. What you know is that nothing in the report lets you check it.
Compare a level-one version: Aisha Rahman, regional officer for the transport union, said the union had been given nine days' notice. Named, with a role, and if it were untrue she could be asked.
grammar.commonMistake: Treating unattributed sourcing as evidence of dishonesty. It exists for real reasons and good journalism uses it. The opposite error is more common and more costly: reading sources say as though it meant several independent people, when it may mean two who heard the same thing from one place.
grammar.memoryTip: Who exactly, and how many. Then find where the main claim sits.
grammar.practice:
For each, say what it fails to tell you and place it on the ladder.
1. Sources say the decision has been taken.
2. It is understood that two sites will close.
3. Critics argue that the policy has failed.
4. There are concerns about the timetable.
5. Aisha Rahman, regional officer for the union, said the notice was nine days.
6. The company said the closures followed a fall in volumes.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Who and how many. Level 4 — undescribed source.
2. Who understands it, and on what basis. Level 5 — no source at all.
3. Which critics, and how many. Level 4, or lower if no critic is ever named.
4. Whose concerns, how many, and how they were measured. Level 5 — concerns is an abstract noun with no owner.
5. Nothing. Level 1 — named person, named role, checkable claim.
6. Nothing about who within the company. Level 2 — a named organisation, which is accountable for its own statement.
Numbers 5 and 6 could both be challenged by going to the named party. Numbers 1 to 4 could not be challenged at all, because there is nobody to go to.
Number 4 is worth noticing as the Unit 8 abstract-noun move applied to opinion: concerns exist without anybody having them.

grammar.title: Both, either and neither
grammar.explanation: Three small words for pairs. The meanings are easy and the agreement and pairings are where the errors are.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
MEANINGS
  BOTH    the two together
     Both sites are closing.
  EITHER  one or the other
     Either site could close.
  NEITHER not one and not the other
     Neither site is closing.

VERB AGREEMENT
  both    -> PLURAL verb
     Both are closing.
  either  -> singular
     Either is acceptable.
  neither -> SINGULAR in careful writing
     Neither is closing.
  ^ you will hear \"neither are\" constantly
    and it is fine in speech. In writing,
    singular is safer.

THE PAIRS
  both ... AND
     both the cost and the timing
  either ... OR
     either Tuesday or Thursday
  neither ... NOR
     neither the cost nor the timing

  NEITHER TAKES NOR, NOT OR.

NEITHER IS ALREADY NEGATIVE
  Neither of them agreed.
  NOT neither of them didn't agree.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say that two things are both problems.
1. Both means the two together, and it takes a plural verb.
2. Result: Both the cost and the timing are problems.
3. Check the pairing: both goes with and, not with or.
Now the negative. Neither thing is a problem.
1. Neither means not one and not the other.
2. It takes nor in the pairing: neither the cost nor the timing.
3. And the verb is singular in careful writing: neither the cost nor the timing is a problem.
4. Check for a doubled negative. Neither already contains the negative, so do not add another — neither of them didn't agree is wrong.
And the middle one. One or the other would do.
1. Either takes or: either Tuesday or Thursday.
2. And a singular verb: either is acceptable.
Three words, three pairings, and the one to remember is that neither takes nor.
grammar.commonMistake: Using neither with or — neither the cost or the timing. It must be nor. The other error is the doubled negative: neither of them didn't agree, which is very common among learners whose first language marks the negative twice. And neither are in formal writing, which is acceptable in speech and looks careless on paper.
grammar.memoryTip: Both and, either or, neither nor. Neither is already negative.
grammar.practice:
Complete each sentence.
1. ____ sites are closing. (the two together)
2. ____ site could close. (one or the other)
3. ____ site is closing. (not one and not the other)
4. ____ the cost ____ the timing is acceptable. (not one and not the other)
5. ____ Tuesday ____ Thursday would do. (one or the other)
6. ____ the cost ____ the timing are problems. (the two together)
grammar.answerKey:
1. Both  2. Either  3. Neither  4. Neither … nor  5. Either … or  6. Both … and
Check the verbs. Number 1 takes are because both is plural. Numbers 3 and 4 take is because neither is singular in careful writing. Number 6 takes are because both is plural.
Number 4 is the one to get right: neither pairs with nor, never with or.
None of these needs a second negative anywhere. Neither carries it already.

grammar.title: Discourse markers
grammar.explanation: Small words that manage a conversation rather than adding information. They are almost entirely spoken, and using them in the wrong register is the main error.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
WHAT THEY DO
  ACTUALLY    corrects gently; adds
              something mildly surprising
     Actually, I think it was Thursday.
  IN FACT     corrects more firmly
     In fact, the figures have doubled.
  MIND YOU    concedes something that
              partly undercuts what you
              just said
     It's expensive. Mind you, it lasts.
  TO BE FAIR  similar, slightly warmer
     To be fair, they did apologise.
  GRANTED     concedes before disagreeing
     Granted, the timing was difficult.
  ANYWAY      closes a digression
  THE THING IS introduces the REAL problem
  FRANKLY     warns that bluntness follows

REGISTER - this is the error
  these are SPOKEN.
  In a report they are wrong.
  Left out of speech, you sound like a
  document.

THEY CARRY NO PARAPHRASABLE MEANING
  they signal what is happening in the
  conversation, not what is true.
grammar.workedExample:
Somebody says the meeting was on Wednesday and you think it was Thursday.
1. You are correcting, and you want it gentle.
2. Actually is the gentle corrector: Actually, I think it was Thursday.
3. Notice you also hedged with I think. The two together make a correction that costs nothing.
4. If you were more certain and the correction mattered more: In fact, it was Thursday — I have the email.
Now a concession that undercuts your own point.
1. You have just said something is expensive.
2. You want to add something that partly argues against you: Mind you, it lasts twice as long.
3. That is not weakness. It signals that you have considered the other side, and it makes the original point more credible.
And the register test. Would any of these belong in a written report? No. A report would say however or nevertheless — the Unit 6 connectors. Actually and mind you in a report read as an unedited transcript.
grammar.commonMistake: Putting spoken markers into formal writing — a report that says mind you or the thing is reads as a transcript rather than a document. The opposite error matters just as much: speech with no markers at all sounds like reading aloud, and learners who have only studied written English often produce exactly that.
grammar.memoryTip: These are for speech. In writing, use the Unit 6 connectors instead.
grammar.practice:
Choose the marker and say whether it belongs in speech or writing.
1. Gently correcting a date.
2. Firmly correcting a figure.
3. Undercutting your own point.
4. Conceding before you disagree.
5. Warning that you are about to be blunt.
6. Ending a digression.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Actually, I think it was Thursday. — speech
2. In fact, the figures have doubled. — speech, though in fact also survives in writing
3. It is expensive. Mind you, it lasts twice as long. — speech only
4. Granted, the timing was difficult. — speech, and granted also appears in argumentative writing
5. Frankly, I do not think it will work. — speech
6. Anyway, what time does it start? — speech only
Numbers 2 and 4 are the two that cross over. In fact and granted both appear in written argument; the others are spoken only.
In a written report, the equivalents come from Unit 6: however for the correction, nevertheless for the concession, and a paragraph break for the digression.

grammar.title: Judging a source
grammar.explanation: Four questions, about thirty seconds. The fourth is the one almost everybody skips, and it is where the commonest error lives.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
1  WHO IS SAYING IT?
     named person / named organisation /
     nobody. (card 1's ladder)

2  HOW DO THEY KNOW?
     were they there? did they see the
     document? or are they passing on
     what somebody else said?
     ^ a person who HEARD about it is
       not a witness.

3  WHAT WOULD THEY GAIN?
     everybody has an interest.
     Having one does NOT make them wrong.
     It tells you which parts to check
     hardest.

4  DOES ANYBODY INDEPENDENT SAY IT?
     REPEATING IS NOT CORROBORATING.

     four outlets in one hour = usually
     ONE press release, briefing or wire.
     One source, printed four times.

     corroboration = an INDEPENDENT PATH
     to the same fact.

     the test: how would EACH outlet have
     found this out? Same route every
     time -> one source.

5  (no answer) WHAT AM I NOT SEEING?
grammar.workedExample:
You see a claim in four different places on the same afternoon and it feels confirmed.
1. Question one: who is saying it? Three of the four say sources say. One names a company statement.
2. Question two: how would they know? Nothing in any of the four says.
3. Question three: what would the source gain? Unknown, because there is no source described.
4. Question four, the important one: how would each outlet have found this out? All four published within an hour of each other, and all four use similar wording.
5. That is not four sources. It is almost certainly one briefing, printed four times.
Now one that does corroborate. A union officer says the notice period was nine days. Separately, the company's published accounts show the volume figures it cited. Those are two independent paths — one person who was in the meeting, and a document that exists regardless of what anybody says.
The difference is not how many places you saw it. It is how many independent routes led there.
grammar.commonMistake: Counting outlets instead of counting sources. Seeing something in four places feels like verification and usually is not. The other error is treating a vested interest as disqualifying — everybody has one, and the useful move is to check the parts of the account that happen to favour the person giving it, rather than dismissing the whole thing.
grammar.memoryTip: Who, how do they know, what would they gain, and who independent says it too.
grammar.practice:
Apply the four questions to each.
1. Four outlets report the same claim within an hour, all saying sources say.
2. A union officer, named, says the notice period was nine days.
3. The company's published accounts show volumes down 11 per cent.
4. A source close to the matter says further closures may follow.
5. Two witnesses who were both present give the same account.
6. A campaigning organisation reports that a policy has failed.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Weak. Nobody named, no basis given, and almost certainly one briefing printed four times. Not corroboration.
2. Strong on questions one and two — named, with a role, and she was party to the notice. Question three: the union has an interest in a longer consultation, so check the nine days against the company's account.
3. Strongest available. A document exists independently of anybody's account and can be checked directly.
4. Weak on every question. Undescribed source, no basis, unknown interest, and may follow is unfalsifiable.
5. Genuine corroboration, provided they did not discuss it first. Two independent paths to the same fact.
6. Credible and interested. A campaigning organisation may be entirely right and has an obvious stake, so question three says check the parts that support its position hardest.
Numbers 3 and 5 are the two forms of real corroboration: a document, and an independent witness. Number 1 is what corroboration usually feels like and is not.

writing.sourceFile: Grade 7 Unit 8, Grade 7 Unit 9; Grade 8 Unit 8
writing.title: Writing 1 — One event, two reports
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Take one event, real or invented.
Write two short reports of it, about 120 words each.
Report A: every claim attributed at level one or two — named people with roles, named organisations, or documents.
Report B: the same event with every claim at level four or five — sources say, it is understood, there are concerns, widely believed.
Nothing untrue in either.
Then write three lines: what B gains by being vague, what it loses, and which claim in B you would most want to check.
writing.modelText:
REPORT A
Northfield Community Centre will close its evening sessions from October, the trustees confirmed on Tuesday. The chair, Ruth Ellis, said the decision followed a 40 per cent fall in evening attendance over two years and the loss of a grant worth 18,000 a year. The centre's published accounts show income down from 96,000 to 71,000 since 2023. Daniel Osei, who runs the Thursday group, said he had been told on Monday and would be looking for another venue. The council said it had not been asked for additional funding.

REPORT B
Sources say Northfield Community Centre is to axe its evening programme, with insiders suggesting the decision was taken months ago. It is understood that funding pressures are behind the move, although there are growing concerns among users that the real reason lies elsewhere. Critics argue the trustees have failed to explore alternatives, and the decision has been widely criticised locally. Further closures may follow. The trustees did not respond to a request for comment.

1. B gains speed, drama and the ability to imply things nobody has said — that the reason given is not the real one, and that more closures are coming.
2. It loses everything checkable: no names, no figures, no documents, and nobody who could be asked whether any of it is true.
3. I would most want to check insiders suggesting the decision was taken months ago, because it is the only claim in B that contradicts the stated account, and it rests on the weakest attribution in the piece.
writing.expectedLength: Two reports of about 120 words plus three lines
writing.successCriteria: Report A attributes every claim at level one or two and includes at least one document; Report B uses at least five vague attributions; both describe the same event and neither contains anything untrue; three lines identifying what vagueness gains, what it costs, and the claim most worth checking
writing.support: Write A first with real names and figures, then convert each sentence downward. Converting shows you exactly what disappears at each step of the ladder.
writing.extension: Count the checkable facts in each. A will have eight or ten and B will have almost none, and both are the same length.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Spoken into written
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a short spoken account of something — six to eight sentences, as you would actually say it, using at least five discourse markers.
Then rewrite it as a written report of the same length, with no discourse markers at all and using Unit 6 connectors instead.
Then write two lines: which markers had no written equivalent, and what the written version lost.
writing.modelText:
SPOKEN
So the delivery didn't turn up on Tuesday. Actually, it turned up on Wednesday but by then we'd already hired a van. Mind you, we'd have hired it anyway because the second job was on the same day. The thing is, nobody told us it was going to be late — that's the bit that annoyed me. Granted, they did ring on Wednesday morning. Frankly I'd rather have known on Monday. Anyway, it's sorted now.

WRITTEN
The delivery did not arrive on Tuesday as scheduled; it arrived on Wednesday. By that point a van had already been hired, although it would probably have been required in any case for a second job on the same date. No notice of the delay was given before Wednesday morning, which is the principal complaint. The supplier did telephone on the Wednesday. Earlier notice would have avoided the additional cost. The matter has since been resolved.

1. Mind you and anyway had no written equivalent at all. Mind you became although, which is close but flatter, and anyway simply disappeared — the written version ends without signalling that it is ending.
2. The written version lost the ranking. In the spoken one, the thing is marks which complaint actually matters; in writing that had to become which is the principal complaint, which states it rather than signalling it.
writing.expectedLength: Two versions of six to eight sentences plus two lines
writing.successCriteria: The spoken version uses at least five different markers naturally; the written version has none and uses connectors from Unit 6 instead; both cover the same content; two lines identifying a marker with no written equivalent and something the written version lost
writing.support: Say the spoken version aloud and transcribe yourself rather than composing it. Composed speech has too few markers, because writing them down feels wrong — which is itself the point.
writing.extension: Read the written version aloud to somebody. It will sound like a document, and that is what speech without markers sounds like.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Place it on the ladder
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write a level from 1 to 5, and say what each fails to tell you.
1. Sources say the decision has been taken.
2. It is understood that two sites will close.
3. Critics argue that the policy has failed.
4. There are concerns about the timetable.
5. Aisha Rahman, regional officer for the union, said the notice was nine days.
6. The company said the closures followed a fall in volumes.
7. A senior manager at the company said the decision was final.
8. The published accounts show volumes down 11 per cent.
9. The move has been widely welcomed.
10. Insiders suggest further closures may follow.
11. A spokesperson for the council confirmed no request had been received.
12. It is believed that staff were not consulted.
activities.answerSummary:
1. Level 4 — who, and how many.
2. Level 5 — who understands it, and on what basis.
3. Level 4 — which critics, and how many.
4. Level 5 — whose concerns; concerns has no owner.
5. Level 1 — nothing missing; named, with a role, on a fact she would know.
6. Level 2 — a named organisation, accountable for its own statement.
7. Level 3 — unnamed but described, so you know the source's position without knowing who they are.
8. Stronger than level 1 — a document exists independently of anybody's account.
9. Level 5 — by whom, and how the width was established.
10. Level 4, and may follow is unfalsifiable as well.
11. Level 2 — a named organisation speaking through a spokesperson.
12. Level 5 — believed by whom.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Apply the four questions
activities.instructionsAndItems:
For each, answer all four questions in one line each.
1. Four outlets report the same claim within an hour, all saying sources say.
2. A union officer, named, says the notice period was nine days.
3. The company's published accounts show volumes down 11 per cent.
4. A source close to the matter says further closures may follow.
5. Two witnesses who were both present give the same account.
6. A campaigning organisation reports that a policy has failed.
7. A photograph, with a date, of the damaged unit.
8. A colleague tells you what somebody in another department said.
activities.answerSummary:
1. Nobody named / no basis given / unknown interest / all four almost certainly from one briefing. One source, not four.
2. Named with a role / she was party to the notice / the union wants a longer consultation, so check the nine days against the company's account / uncorroborated so far.
3. A published document / it exists independently of anybody's account / the company prepared it, so it is audited but not disinterested / it can be checked directly.
4. Undescribed / no basis / unknown / and may follow cannot be falsified in any case.
5. Two named people / both present / interests unknown / genuine corroboration, provided they did not discuss it first.
6. A named organisation / depends on their method / an obvious stake, so check the parts supporting their position hardest / credible and interested are both true.
7. A document of a kind / it records a state at a time / whoever took it chose the framing / strong on the fact of damage, silent on the cause.
8. Your colleague heard it / they were not present, so this is second-hand / unknown / not a source at all in the sense that matters.
Numbers 3 and 7 are documents, and both are strong on what they record and silent on why. A photograph shows damage and not its cause.
Number 8 is the one worth dwelling on: somebody repeating what they heard is not a witness, and reports often describe exactly this as a source familiar with the matter.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Track one story
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Take one news story and find it in three different places.
For each version, write down: the headline, the strongest source it cites, and its weakest.
Then ask how each outlet would have found the story out.
Write two lines: whether you found three sources or one, and where the headlines differed most from the articles beneath them.
activities.answerSummary:
No key — it is your story.
What most people find: three versions and one source. If the story broke the same day, all three usually trace to a statement, a wire service or a briefing, and the wording similarities give it away.
The second finding is about headlines. Headlines are frequently stronger than the articles beneath them, and they are usually written by somebody other than the reporter. A headline that states a claim flatly above an article that hedges it three times is extremely common, and noticing the gap is a useful reading habit.
The third finding, which surprises people: the strongest source is often buried in the middle of the piece and the weakest is near the top, because the unattributed claim is what makes the story new.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Compare two feeds
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Ask somebody to describe the first ten things they saw on a platform they use, and describe your own ten.
Write down how many overlap.
Then note what kinds of thing appear in theirs that never appear in yours.
Write one line on what you concluded.
Do not share any personal content or accounts — only the general categories.
activities.answerSummary:
No key.
What most people find: almost no overlap, even between people who use the same platform in the same place on the same day. Two or three out of ten is common and zero is not unusual.
The second finding is the point of the exercise. The selection is invisible from inside it — your feed feels like what is happening, and so does theirs. Neither is, and no amount of scrolling reveals the shape of what was left out.
The third finding is worth holding on to. This is not an argument for distrusting everything you see. It is an argument for knowing that the question what am I not seeing has no answer available from inside the feed, and that occasionally looking at somebody else's is the only cheap way to get any answer at all.

11. Nevertheless, or although — the written equivalent of mind you
12. A paragraph break, or turning to — writing has no direct equivalent of anyway
Only in fact and granted cross over comfortably. Everything else is spoken, and the written equivalents come from Unit 6 rather than from this card.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. Nobody named / no basis given / unknown interest / all four almost certainly from one briefing. One source, not four.
2. Named with a role / she was party to the notice / the union wants a longer consultation, so check the nine days against the company's account / uncorroborated so far.
3. A published document / it exists independently of anybody's account / the company prepared it, so it is audited but not disinterested / it can be checked directly.
4. Undescribed / no basis / unknown / and may follow cannot be falsified in any case.
5. Two named people / both present / interests unknown / genuine corroboration, provided they did not discuss it first.
6. A named organisation / depends on their method / an obvious stake, so check the parts supporting their position hardest / credible and interested are both true.
7. A document of a kind / it records a state at a time / whoever took it chose the framing / strong on the fact of damage, silent on the cause.
8. Your colleague heard it / they were not present, so this is second-hand / unknown / not a source at all in the sense that matters.
Numbers 3 and 7 are documents, and both are strong on what they record and silent on why. A photograph shows damage and not its cause.
Number 8 is the one worth dwelling on: somebody repeating what they heard is not a witness, and reports often describe exactly this as a source familiar with the matter.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
No key — it is your story.
What most people find: three versions and one source. If the story broke the same day, all three usually trace to a statement, a wire service or a briefing, and the wording similarities give it away.
The second finding is about headlines. Headlines are frequently stronger than the articles beneath them, and they are usually written by somebody other than the reporter. A headline that states a claim flatly above an article that hedges it three times is extremely common, and noticing the gap is a useful reading habit.
The third finding, which surprises people: the strongest source is often buried in the middle of the piece and the weakest is near the top, because the unattributed claim is what makes the story new.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
No key.
What most people find: almost no overlap, even between people who use the same platform in the same place on the same day. Two or three out of ten is common and zero is not unusual.
The second finding is the point of the exercise. The selection is invisible from inside it — your feed feels like what is happening, and so does theirs. Neither is, and no amount of scrolling reveals the shape of what was left out.
The third finding is worth holding on to. This is not an argument for distrusting everything you see. It is an argument for knowing that the question what am I not seeing has no answer available from inside the feed, and that occasionally looking at somebody else's is the only cheap way to get any answer at all.
